response.text:
## Chapter 1 — Enter Ahab; to Him, Stubb.

Some days elapsed, ice and icebergs all astern, the Pequod went rolling through the bright Quito spring, which, at sea, almost perpetually reigns on the threshold of the eternal August of the Tropic. The clear, ringing days were as crystal goblets of Persian sherbet, heaped up with rose-water snow; the starred and stately nights seemed haughty dames in jewelled velvets, nursing in lonely pride the memory of their absent conquering Earls. And all these subtle agencies wrought on Ahab's texture.

Old age is always wakeful; as if, the longer linked with life, the less man has to do with aught that looks like death. So with Ahab: of late he seemed to live in the open air. "It feels like going down into one's tomb," he would mutter, "for an old captain like me to be descending this narrow scuttle, to my grave-dug berth."

Almost every twenty-four hours the silent steersman would watch the cabin-scuttle, and ere long the old man would emerge, gripping the iron banister to help his crippled way. He usually abstained from patrolling the quarter-deck, lest the crack of his bony step disturb his mates' dreams. But once the mood was on him too deep for common regardings; and as he measured the ship with heavy, lumber-like pace, Stubb came up and hinted that if the Captain pleased to walk the planks, no one could say nay; but there might be some way of muffling the noise — something about a globe of tow, and the insertion of the ivory heel.

"Am I a cannon-ball, Stubb," said Ahab, "that thou wouldst wad me that fashion? But go thy ways; I had forgot. Below to thy nightly grave; where such as ye sleep between shrouds, to use ye to the filling one at last. — Down, dog, and kennel!"

Stubb was speechless a moment; then said excitedly, "I am not used to be spoken to that way, sir; I do but less than half like it."

"Avast!" gritted Ahab, moving violently away as if to avoid some passionate temptation.

"No, sir; not yet," said Stubb, emboldened, "I will not tamely be called a dog, sir."

"Then be called ten times a donkey, and a mule, and an ass, and begone, or I'll clear the world of thee!"

As he said this, Ahab advanced upon him with such overbearing terrors in his aspect that Stubb involuntarily retreated.

"I was never served so before without giving a hard blow for it," muttered Stubb, descending the cabin-scuttle. "Somehow, I don't well know whether to go back and strike him, or — down here on my knees and pray for him? It would be the first time I ever _did_ pray. He's the queerest old man Stubb ever sailed with. How he flashed at me! — his eyes like powder-pans! There's something on his mind. He aint in his bed three hours out of the twenty-four; the steward says his pillow's always frightful hot, as though a baked brick had been on it. A hot old man! I guess he's got what some folks ashore call a conscience; a kind of Tic-Dolly-row they say — worse nor a toothache. What does he go into the after hold for, every night? Who's made appointments with him there? Think not, is my eleventh commandment; and sleep when you can, is my twelfth. But he called me ten times a donkey, and piled a lot of jackasses on top of _that!_ That old man has turned me wrong side out. The only way's to stash it; in the morning, I'll see how this plaguey juggling thinks over by daylight."

---

## Chapter 2 — The Pipe.

After Stubb departed, Ahab sent below for his ivory stool and pipe; lighting it at the binnacle lamp, he sat and smoked.

In old Norse times, the thrones of the sea-loving Danish kings were fabricated of the tusks of the narwhale. Seated on that tripod of bones, Ahab seemed a Khan of the plank, a king of the sea, a great lord of Leviathans.

"How now," he soliloquized at last, "this smoking no longer soothes. Oh, my pipe! hard must it go with me if thy charm be gone! This thing meant for sereneness, to send up mild white vapors among mild white hairs, not among torn iron-grey locks like mine. I'll smoke no more —"

He tossed the still lighted pipe into the sea. The fire hissed in the waves; the ship shot by the bubble the sinking pipe made. With slouched hat, Ahab lurchingly paced the planks.

---

## Chapter 3 — Queen Mab.

Next morning Stubb accosted Flask.

"Such a queer dream, King-Post, I never had. You know the old man's ivory leg? I dreamed he kicked me with it; and when I tried to kick back, I kicked my leg right off! Then, presto! Ahab seemed a pyramid, and I, like a blazing fool, kept kicking at it. But all the while I thought it not much of an insult — 'not a real leg, only a false leg. There's a mighty difference between a living thump and a dead thump. What's his leg but a cane — a whalebone cane. Only a playful cudgelling — only a whaleboning.' But now comes the greatest joke. While I was battering at the pyramid, a sort of badger-haired old merman, with a hump on his back, takes me by the shoulders and slews me round. 'What are you 'bout?' says he. Such a phiz! 'What am I about?' says I. 'What business is that of yours, Mr. Humpback? Do _you_ want a kick?' Lord, Flask, no sooner had I said that, than he turned his stern to me, dragged up a clout of seaweed — and his stern was stuck full of marlinspikes, points out. 'I guess I won't kick you, old fellow.' 'Wise Stubb,' said he, 'wise Stubb;' muttering it like a chimney hag. Then: 'let's argue the insult. Captain Ahab kicked ye with his ivory leg, didn't he? Well then, wise Stubb, what have you to complain of? Ye were kicked by a great man, and with a beautiful ivory leg. It's an honor. In old England lords think it great glory to be slapped by a queen, and made garter-knights of; but be _your_ boast, Stubb, that ye were kicked by old Ahab, and made a wise man of. Account his kicks honors; and on no account kick back; for you can't help yourself, wise Stubb.' With that, he swam off into the air. I snored, and there I was in my hammock. What do you think of that dream, Flask?"

"I don't know; it seems a sort of foolish to me, tho.'"

"May be; but it's made a wise man of me. The best thing you can do is to let the old man alone; never speak to him, whatever he says. Halloa! What's that he shouts? Hark!"

"Mast-head, there! Look sharp, all of ye! There are whales hereabouts!

"If ye see a white one, split your lungs for him!"

"What do you think of that now, Flask? A white whale — did ye mark that, man? There's something special in the wind. Ahab has that that's bloody on his mind. But, mum; he comes this way."

---

## Chapter 4 — Cetology.

Already we are boldly launched upon the deep; but soon we shall be lost in its unshored, harbourless immensities. Ere that come to pass, it is well to attend to a matter almost indispensable to a thorough appreciative understanding of the more special leviathanic revelations and allusions which are to follow.

It is some systematized exhibition of the whale in his broad genera that I would now fain put before you. Yet is it no easy task. The classification of the constituents of a chaos, nothing less is here essayed.

"No branch of Zoology is so much involved as that which is entitled Cetology," says Captain Scoresby, A.D. 1820. "Utter confusion exists among the historians of this animal," says Surgeon Beale, A.D. 1839. "Unfitness to pursue our research in the unfathomable waters." "Impenetrable veil covering our knowledge of the cetacea." "A field strewn with thorns." Thus speak Cuvier, John Hunter, and Lesson, those lights of zoology and anatomy. Nevertheless, though of real knowledge there be little, yet of books there are a plenty. Many are the men who have written of the whale: the Authors of the Bible; Aristotle; Pliny; Sir Thomas Browne; Linnæus; Cuvier; Hunter; Owen; Scoresby; Beale; Bennett; the Author of Miriam Coffin. Yet only Scoresby was a real professional whaleman, and he says nothing of the great sperm whale, compared with which the Greenland whale is almost unworthy mentioning. The Greenland whale is an usurper upon the throne of the seas. Reference to nearly all the leviathanic allusions in the great poets of past days will satisfy you that the Greenland whale was to them the monarch of the seas. But the time has at last come for a new proclamation. This is Charing Cross; hear ye! good people all — the Greenland whale is deposed; the great sperm whale now reigneth!

There are only two books in being which at all pretend to put the living sperm whale before you, and at the same time succeed in the attempt: Beale's and Bennett's, both surgeons to English South-Sea whale-ships. As yet, however, the sperm whale, scientific or poetic, lives not complete in any literature. Far above all other hunted whales, his is an unwritten life.

The various species of whales need some sort of popular comprehensive classification, if only an easy outline one. As no better man advances to take this matter in hand, I hereupon offer my own poor endeavors. I promise nothing complete; because any human thing supposed to be complete, must for that very reason infallibly be faulty. My object here is simply to project the draught of a systematization of cetology. _I am the architect, not the builder._

But it is a ponderous task. To grope down into the bottom of the sea; to have one's hands among the unspeakable foundations, ribs, and very pelvis of the world; this is a fearful thing. What am I that I should essay to hook the nose of this leviathan! The awful tauntings in Job might well appal me. Will he (the leviathan) make a covenant with thee? Behold the hope of him is vain! But I have swam through libraries and sailed through oceans; I have had to do with whales with these visible hands; I am in earnest; and I will try.

First: The uncertain, unsettled condition of this science is in the very vestibule attested by the fact that in some quarters it still remains a moot point whether a whale be a fish. In his System of Nature, A.D. 1776, Linnæus declares, "I hereby separate the whales from the fish." But of my own knowledge, I know that down to the year 1850, sharks and shad, alewives and herring, against Linnæus's express edict, were still found dividing the possession of the same seas with the Leviathan.

The grounds upon which Linnæus would fain have banished the whales he states as follows: "On account of their warm bilocular heart, their lungs, their movable eyelids, their hollow ears, _penem intrantem feminam mammis lactantem_," and finally, "_ex lege naturæ jure meritoque_." I submitted all this to my friends Simeon Macey and Charley Coffin, of Nantucket, and they united in the opinion that the reasons set forth were altogether insufficient. Charley profanely hinted they were humbug.

Be it known that, waiving all argument, I take the good old fashioned ground that the whale is a fish, and call upon holy Jonah to back me. Next: how shall we define the whale, by his obvious externals, so as conspicuously to label him for all time to come? To be short, then, _a whale is a spouting fish with a horizontal tail._ There you have him. However contracted, that definition is the result of expanded meditation. A walrus spouts much like a whale, but the walrus is not a fish, because he is amphibious. And among spouting fish the tail, though it may be similarly shaped, invariably assumes a horizontal position. Now, then, come the grand divisions of the entire whale host.

According to magnitude I divide the whales into three primary BOOKS (subdivisible into CHAPTERS), and these shall comprehend them all, both small and large.

I. THE FOLIO WHALE; II. the OCTAVO WHALE; III. the DUODECIMO WHALE.

As the type of the FOLIO I present the _Sperm Whale_; of the OCTAVO, the _Grampus_; of the DUODECIMO, the _Porpoise_.

FOLIOS. — I. The _Sperm Whale_; II. the _Right Whale_; III. the _Fin-Back Whale_; IV. the _Hump-backed Whale_; V. the _Razor Back Whale_; VI. the _Sulphur Bottom Whale_.

BOOK I. (_Folio_), CHAPTER I. (_Sperm Whale_). — This whale, the present Cachalot of the French, the Pottsfich of the Germans, the Macrocephalus of the Long Words, is, without doubt, the largest inhabitant of the globe; the most formidable of all whales to encounter; the most majestic in aspect; and lastly, by far the most valuable in commerce; he being the only creature from which that valuable substance, spermaceti, is obtained. Philologically considered, his name is absurd. Some centuries ago, when the sperm whale was almost wholly unknown in his own proper individuality, spermaceti was popularly supposed to be derived from a creature identical with the Greenland or Right Whale. When the true nature of spermaceti became known, its original name was still retained, and the appellation must at last have come to be bestowed upon the whale from which this spermaceti was really derived.

BOOK I. (_Folio_), CHAPTER II. (_Right Whale_). — In one respect this is the most venerable of the leviathans, being the one first regularly hunted by man. It yields the article commonly known as whalebone or baleen; and the oil specially known as "whale oil," an inferior article in commerce. Among the fishermen, he is indiscriminately designated by all the following titles: The Whale; the Greenland Whale; the Black Whale; the Great Whale; the True Whale; the Right Whale. Some pretend to see a difference between the Greenland whale of the English and the right whale of the Americans. But they precisely agree in all their grand features.

BOOK I. (_Folio_), CHAPTER III. (_Fin-Back_). — Under this head I reckon a monster which, by the various names of Fin-Back, Tall-Spout, and Long-John, has been seen almost in every sea. His grand distinguishing feature, the fin, from which he derives his name, is some three or four feet long, growing vertically from the hinder part of the back, of an angular shape, and with a very sharp pointed end. When the sea is moderately calm, this gnomon-like fin stands up and casts shadows upon the wrinkled surface; the watery circle surrounding it somewhat resembles a dial, with its style and wavy hour-lines graved on it. On that Ahaz-dial the shadow often goes back. The Fin-Back is not gregarious. He seems a whale-hater, as some men are man-haters. Very shy; always going solitary; unexpectedly rising to the surface in the remotest and most sullen waters; his straight and single lofty jet rising like a tall misanthropic spear upon a barren plain; this leviathan seems the banished and unconquerable Cain of his race, bearing for his mark that style upon his back.

In connection with this appellative of "Whalebone whales," it is of great importance to mention, that however such a nomenclature may be convenient, yet it is in vain to attempt a clear classification of the Leviathan, founded upon either his baleen, or hump, or fin, or teeth. The baleen, hump, back-fin, and teeth — these are things whose peculiarities are indiscriminately dispersed among all sorts of whales. The sperm whale and the humpbacked whale, each has a hump; but there the similitude ceases. On this rock every one of the whale-naturalists has split. What then remains? nothing but to take hold of the whales bodily, in their entire liberal volume, and boldly sort them that way. And this is the Bibliographical system here adopted.

BOOK I. (_Folio_) CHAPTER IV. (_Hump Back_). — This whale is often seen on the northern American coast. He has a great pack on him like a peddler; or you might call him the Elephant and Castle whale. He is the most gamesome and light-hearted of all the whales, making more gay foam and white water generally than any other of them.

BOOK I. (_Folio_), CHAPTER V. (_Razor Back_). — Of this whale little is known but his name. I have seen him at a distance off Cape Horn. Of a retiring nature, he eludes both hunters and philosophers. Though no coward, he has never yet shown any part of him but his back, which rises in a long sharp ridge. Let him go.

BOOK I. (_Folio_), CHAPTER VI. (_Sulphur Bottom_). — Another retiring gentleman, with a brimstone belly, doubtless got by scraping along the Tartarian tiles in some of his profounder divings. He is seldom seen; he is never chased; he would run away with rope-walks of line. Adieu, Sulphur Bottom! I can say nothing more that is true of ye.

Thus ends BOOK I. (_Folio_), and now begins BOOK II. (_Octavo_).

OCTAVOES. — These embrace the whales of middling magnitude, among which present may be numbered: I., the _Grampus_; II., the _Black Fish_; III., the _Narwhale_; IV., the _Thrasher_; V., the _Killer_.

BOOK II. (_Octavo_), CHAPTER I. (_Grampus_). — Though this fish, whose loud sonorous breathing has furnished a proverb to landsmen, is not popularly classed among whales, most naturalists have recognised him for one. He is of moderate octavo size, varying from fifteen to twenty-five feet in length. He swims in herds; his approach is regarded as premonitory of the advance of the great sperm whale.

BOOK II. (_Octavo_), CHAPTER II. (_Black Fish_). — Where any name happens to be vague or inexpressive, I shall suggest another. Call him the Hyena Whale. From the circumstance that the inner angles of his lips are curved upwards, he carries an everlasting Mephistophelean grin on his face. When not more profitably employed, the sperm whale hunters sometimes capture the Hyena whale, to keep up the supply of cheap oil for domestic employment — as some frugal housekeepers, in the absence of company, burn unsavory tallow instead of odorous wax.

BOOK II. (_Octavo_), CHAPTER III. (_Narwhale_), that is, _Nostril whale_. — Another instance of a curiously named whale, so named I suppose from his peculiar horn being originally mistaken for a peaked nose. The creature is some sixteen feet in length, while its horn averages five feet, though some attain to fifteen. Strictly speaking, this horn is but a lengthened tusk, growing out from the jaw, found only on the sinister side, giving its owner something analogous to the aspect of a clumsy left-handed man. What precise purpose this ivory horn answers, it would be hard to say. My own opinion is that it would certainly be very convenient to him for a folder in reading pamphlets. From certain cloistered old authors I have gathered that this same sea-unicorn's horn was in ancient days regarded as the great antidote against poison, and as such, preparations of it brought immense prices. Black Letter tells me that Sir Martin Frobisher on his return from that voyage, when Queen Bess did gallantly wave her jewelled hand to him from a window of Greenwich Palace, "on bended knees he presented to her highness a prodigious long horn of the Narwhale, which for a long period after hung in the castle at Windsor."

BOOK II. (_Octavo_), CHAPTER IV. (_Killer_). — Of this whale little is precisely known. He is very savage — a sort of Feegee fish. He sometimes takes the great Folio whales by the lip, and hangs there like a leech, till the mighty brute is worried to death. Exception might be taken to the name bestowed upon this whale, on the ground of its indistinctness. For we are all killers, on land and on sea; Bonapartes and Sharks included.

BOOK II. (_Octavo_), CHAPTER V. (_Thrasher_). — This gentleman is famous for his tail, which he uses for a ferule in thrashing his foes. He mounts the Folio whale's back, and as he swims, he works his passage by flogging him; as some schoolmasters get along in the world by a similar process. Both are outlaws, even in the lawless seas.

Thus ends BOOK II. (_Octavo_), and begins BOOK III. (_Duodecimo_).

DUODECIMOES. — These include the smaller whales. I. The Huzza Porpoise. II. The Algerine Porpoise. III. The Mealy-mouthed Porpoise.

BOOK III. (_Duodecimo_), CHAPTER 1. (_Huzza Porpoise_). — This is the common porpoise found almost all over the globe. The name is of my own bestowal. I call him thus, because he always swims in hilarious shoals, which upon the broad sea keep tossing themselves to heaven like caps in a Fourth-of-July crowd. They are the lads that always live before the wind. They are accounted a lucky omen. If you yourself can withstand three cheers at beholding these vivacious fish, then heaven help ye; the spirit of godly gamesomeness is not in ye.

BOOK III. (_Duodecimo_), CHAPTER II. (_Algerine Porpoise_). — A pirate. Very savage. He is only found, I think, in the Pacific. Provoke him, and he will buckle to a shark.

BOOK III. (_Duodecimo_), CHAPTER III. (_Mealy-mouthed Porpoise_). — The largest kind of Porpoise, and only found in the Pacific. He has a lovely tail, and sentimental Indian eyes of a hazel hue. But his mealy-mouth spoils all. A boundary line streaks him from stem to stern with two separate colours, black above and white below; the white comprises the whole of his mouth, which makes him look as if he had just escaped from a felonious visit to a meal-bag. A most mean and mealy aspect!

Beyond the DUODECIMO this system does not proceed. Above, you have all the Leviathans of note. But there are a rabble of uncertain, fugitive, half-fabulous whales — The Bottle-Nose Whale; the Junk Whale; the Pudding-Headed Whale; the Cape Whale; the Leading Whale; the Cannon Whale; the Scragg Whale; the Coppered Whale; the Elephant Whale; the Iceberg Whale; the Quog Whale; the Blue Whale — names full of Leviathanism, but signifying nothing.

Finally: It was stated at the outset that this system would not be here, and at once, perfected. You cannot but plainly see that I have kept my word. I now leave my cetological System standing thus unfinished, even as the great Cathedral of Cologne was left, with the crane still standing upon the top of the uncompleted tower. For small erections may be finished by their first architects; grand ones, true ones, ever leave the copestone to posterity. _God keep me from ever completing anything._ This whole book is but a draught — nay, but the draught of a draught. Oh, Time, Strength, Cash, and Patience!

---

## Chapter 5 — The Specksnyder.

Concerning the officers of the whale-craft, set down a little peculiarity arising from the existence of the harpooneer class, unknown in any other marine than the whale-fleet.

The importance attached to the harpooneer's vocation is evinced by the fact that originally in the old Dutch Fishery, two centuries and more ago, the command of a whale ship was divided between the captain and an officer called the Specksnyder. Literally Fat-Cutter; usage made it equivalent to Chief Harpooneer. The captain's authority was restricted to navigation; over the whale-hunting department the Specksnyder reigned supreme. In the British Greenland Fishery, under the corrupted title of Specksioneer, this old Dutch official is still retained, but his former dignity is sadly abridged. In the American Fishery the harpooneer is not only an important officer in the boat, but under certain circumstances the command of the ship's deck is also his; therefore the grand political maxim of the sea demands that he should nominally live apart from the men before the mast, though always, by them, familiarly regarded as their social equal.

The grand distinction drawn between officer and man at sea is this — the first lives aft, the last forward. Hence, in most American whalers the harpooneers are lodged aft: they take their meals in the captain's cabin and sleep in a place indirectly communicating with it.

Though the long period of a Southern whaling voyage, its peculiar perils, and the community of interest among a company who depend for their profits not upon fixed wages but upon their common luck, do beget a less rigorous discipline than in merchantmen generally; yet the punctilious externals of the quarter-deck are seldom relaxed. Many are the Nantucket ships in which you will see the skipper parading his quarter-deck with an elated grandeur not surpassed in any military navy.

Of all men the moody captain of the Pequod was the least given to that shallowest assumption; the only homage he ever exacted was implicit, instantaneous obedience; yet even Captain Ahab was by no means unobservant of the paramount forms and usages of the sea.

Nor will it fail to be eventually perceived that behind those forms and usages he sometimes masked himself, incidentally making use of them for other and more private ends than they were legitimately intended to subserve. That certain sultanism of his brain, which had otherwise remained unmanifested, through those forms became incarnate in an irresistible dictatorship. For be a man's intellectual superiority what it will, it can never assume the practical, available supremacy over other men, without the aid of some sort of external arts and entrenchments, always, in themselves, more or less paltry and base. This it is that for ever keeps God's true princes of the Empire from the world's hustings.

But Ahab, my Captain, still moves before me in all his Nantucket grimness and shagginess; and in this episode touching Emperors and Kings, I must not conceal that I have only to do with a poor old whale-hunter like him; and therefore all outward majestical trappings and housings are denied me. Oh, Ahab! what shall be grand in thee, it must needs be plucked at from the skies, and dived for in the deep, and featured in the unbodied air!

---

## Chapter 6 — The Cabin-Table.

It is noon; Dough-Boy, the steward, thrusting his pale loaf-of-bread face from the cabin-scuttle, announces dinner to his lord and master; who, sitting in the lee quarter-boat, has just been taking an observation of the sun, mutely reckoning the latitude on the smooth tablet on the upper part of his ivory leg. From his complete inattention to the tidings, you would think that moody Ahab had not heard. But presently he swings himself to the deck, and in an even, unexhilarated voice, saying, "Dinner, Mr. Starbuck," disappears into the cabin.

When the last echo of his sultan's step has died away, Starbuck, the first Emir, takes a few turns along the planks, and, after a grave peep into the binnacle, says, "Dinner, Mr. Stubb," and descends. The second Emir lounges about the rigging awhile, then takes up the old burden — "Dinner, Mr. Flask" — and follows.

But the third Emir, now seeing himself alone on the quarter-deck, seems relieved from some curious restraint; tipping winks in all directions and kicking off his shoes, he strikes into a noiseless squall of a hornpipe right over the Grand Turk's head. But ere stepping into the cabin, he pauses, ships a new face altogether, and then independent, hilarious little Flask enters King Ahab's presence, in the character of Abjectus, or the Slave.

It is not the least among the strange things bred by the intense artificialness of sea-usages, that while in the open air some officers will, upon provocation, bear themselves boldly enough towards their commander, yet at dinner in that same cabin their air towards him is deprecatory, sometimes most comical. To have been Belshazzar, King of Babylon — not haughtily but courteously — therein must have been some touch of mundane grandeur. Who has but once dined his friends, has tasted what it is to be Cæsar. Superadd to this the official supremacy of a ship-master, and you derive the cause of that peculiarity of sea-life.

Over his ivory-inlaid table, Ahab presided like a mute, maned sea-lion on the white coral beach, surrounded by his warlike but still deferential cubs. They were as little children before Ahab; and yet, in Ahab, there seemed not to lurk the smallest social arrogance. With one mind, their intent eyes fastened upon the old man's knife as he carved. They would not have profaned that moment with the slightest observation, even upon so neutral a topic as the weather. When Ahab motioned Starbuck's plate towards him, the mate received his meat as though receiving alms, cut it tenderly, and chewed it noiselessly. These cabin meals were solemn meals, eaten in awful silence; yet old Ahab forbade not conversation; only he himself was dumb. What a relief it was to choking Stubb when a rat made a sudden racket in the hold below.

And poor little Flask, he was the youngest son, and little boy of this weary family party. His were the shinbones of the saline beef. For Flask to have presumed to help himself must have seemed tantamount to larceny in the first degree. Least of all did Flask presume to help himself to butter. Whether he thought the owners denied it to him on account of its clotting his clear, sunny complexion; or whether he deemed that, on so long a voyage, butter was at a premium and not for a subaltern; however it was, Flask, alas! was a butterless man!

Flask was the last person down at the dinner, and the first man up. If Stubb, who is but a peg higher, happens to have a small appetite, Flask gets no more than three mouthfuls; for it is against holy usage for Stubb to precede Flask to the deck. Flask once admitted in private that ever since he had arisen to the dignity of an officer, he had never known what it was to be otherwise than hungry. Besides, if any sailor had a grudge against Flask, all he had to do was go aft at dinner-time and get a peep at Flask through the cabin sky-light, sitting silly and dumfoundered before awful Ahab.

After Ahab and his three mates departed in inverted order to their arrival, the three harpooneers were bidden to the feast, they being its residuary legatees. They made a sort of temporary servants' hall of the high and mighty cabin.

In strange contrast to the hardly tolerable constraint of the captain's table, was the entire care-free license and ease, the almost frantic democracy of those inferior fellows the harpooneers. While their masters seemed afraid of the sound of the hinges of their own jaws, the harpooneers chewed their food with such a relish that there was a report to it. They dined like lords; they filled their bellies like Indian ships all day loading with spices. Such portentous appetites had Queequeg and Tashtego, that to fill out the vacancies the pale Dough-Boy was fain to bring on a great baron of salt-junk. If he were not lively, Tashtego had an ungentlemanly way of accelerating him by darting a fork at his back, harpoon-wise. Once Daggoo, seized with a sudden humor, snatched Dough-Boy up bodily and thrust his head into an empty wooden trencher, while Tashtego, knife in hand, began laying out the circle preliminary to scalping him. What with the standing spectacle of the black terrific Ahab, and the tumultuous visitations of these three savages, Dough-Boy's whole life was one continual lip-quiver.

It was a sight to see Queequeg seated over against Tashtego, opposing his filed teeth to the Indian's; crosswise to them, Daggoo on the floor, for a bench would have brought his hearse-plumed head to the low carlines. But the great negro was wonderfully abstemious; doubtless this noble savage fed strong and drank deep of the abounding element of air, and through his dilated nostrils snuffed in the sublime life of the worlds. Queequeg, he had a mortal, barbaric smack of the lip in eating — so much so that the trembling Dough-Boy almost looked to see whether any marks of teeth lurked in his own lean arms. Hard fares the white waiter who waits upon cannibals.

Though these barbarians dined in the cabin, they were scarcely ever in it except at mealtimes. Ahab seemed no exception to most American whale captains, who incline to the opinion that by rights the ship's cabin belongs to them. The mates and harpooneers of the Pequod might more properly be said to have lived out of the cabin than in it. Nor did they lose much hereby; in the cabin was no companionship; socially, Ahab was inaccessible. Though nominally included in the census of Christendom, he was still an alien to it. He lived in the world, as the last of the Grisly Bears lived in settled Missouri. And as when Spring and Summer had departed, that wild Logan of the woods, burying himself in the hollow of a tree, lived out the winter there, sucking his own paws; so, in his inclement, howling old age, Ahab's soul, shut up in the caved trunk of his body, there fed upon the sullen paws of its gloom!
